annotations.annotation_text: Page 15 opens Book 1, Chapter 1 ("The Fall of Finnegan") during the Age of Gods (Theocratic) phase. This passage continues the mythic fall of Tim Finnegan / HCE, the thunderclap awakening primitive religion, and the recumbent giant embedded in the Dublin landscape, featuring HCE, Finn MacCool, Mutt and Jute. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8

JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: Portmanteau "laughtears" (015.09): fused coinage of laughter and tears, expressing Joyce's core aesthetic philosophy that human history is simultaneously farcical and heartbreaking, a tragicomic drama where weeping and laughing dissolve into a single visceral response.
sources: McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Beckett, Samuel. Dante... Bruno. Vico.. Joyce. https://archive.org/details/ourexagminationr0000unse

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 15 ("The Fall of Finnegan"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods (Theocratic) dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind

annotations.annotation_text: Mutt and Jute dialogue opening (015.29): prehistoric encounter between Mutt (indigenous Celtic/aboriginal inhabitant, mute and impoverished) and Jute (Jute/Norse/Saxon invader). Set on the battlefield of Clontarf (1014), the dialogue dramatizes the breakdown of linguistic communication between conqueror and native.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
FWEET: Mutt and Jute concordance. https://www.fweet.org
Curtis, Edmund. A History of Ireland. https://archive.org/details/historyofireland0000curt

annotations.annotation_text: Megalithic anchor "lith stone" (015.31): Greek 'lithos' (stone) fused with English 'stone', denoting a prehistoric cromlech or standing stone on the Dublin strand. In Viconian terms, the dialogue takes place upon the immobile mineral bedrock of ancient Ireland.
sources: Contemporary Literature Press: Classical Lexicon for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Mink, Louis O. A Finnegans Wake Gazetteer. https://archive.org/details/finneganswakegaz0000mink

annotations.annotation_text: Linguistic distortion "poposterous" (015.33): preposterous + post-posterity. Highlights the absurd, anachronistic nature of this prehistoric archaeological dialogue where modern Dublin dialect echoes through prehistoric bog-matter.

Comic-strip structure (015.35): Joyce models Mutt and Jute directly on Bud Fisher's famous early 20th-century newspaper comic strip 'Mutt and Jeff', collapsing mass-market American Sunday funnies into the prehistoric strata of Irish archaeology.
sources: Norris, Margot. The Decentered Universe of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/decentereduniver0000norr
